nameStory: This sweet-smelling vine gets its name from its native home in Japan and East Asia, plus the honeyed fragrance of its tubular flowers. The alternative name 'golden-and-silver honeysuckle' comes from how the creamy white flowers age to golden yellow, creating a two-toned display on the same vine.
description: Japanese honeysuckle is a vigorous, semi-evergreen vine that can climb 30 feet or more up trees, fences, and other supports. It produces pairs of fragrant, trumpet-shaped flowers that start white and turn yellow with age, blooming from late spring through fall. The oval leaves stay green well into winter in mild years, and the vine spreads aggressively both by climbing and by sending out runners along the ground.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tubular, trumpet-shaped flowers appear in pairs, starting creamy white and aging to golden yellow - you'll often see both colors on the same vine. The flowers have a sweet, almost vanilla-like fragrance that's strongest in the evening and can be detected from several feet away.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Oval leaves grow in opposite pairs along the vine and feel slightly fuzzy when young, becoming smoother with age. Unlike most vines, the leaves stay green well into winter, turning purplish in cold weather but rarely dropping completely.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: A twining vine that spirals clockwise around supports, also spreading along the ground with rooting runners. The stems feel slightly hairy when young and become smooth and woody with hollow centers as they mature.

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Small black berries appear in pairs where the flowers were, ripening in late summer. The berries are about the size of a peppercorn and have a somewhat bitter taste.

habitat: Japanese honeysuckle thrives in forest edges, abandoned fields, roadsides, and disturbed areas throughout New England. It tolerates both sun and shade but grows most vigorously in partially sunny spots with moist, well-drained soil. You'll often find it smothering native understory plants and climbing high into tree canopies.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges early with fresh green leaves, and the first fragrant white flowers appear in late spring. This is when the sweet evening fragrance is most noticeable.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming period with continuous flowers from white to yellow stages, followed by small black berries in late summer. The vine grows most aggressively during hot weather.
seasonality.fall: Flowering often continues into fall, and leaves may turn purplish but typically remain attached. Late-season berries provide food for birds who help spread the seeds.
seasonality.winter: Semi-evergreen leaves persist in mild winters, turning bronze or purplish. The woody stems with their hollow centers and opposite branching pattern are visible, along with any remaining berries.

funFact: Japanese honeysuckle flowers are edible and have been used to make tea, wine, and even ice cream - but only harvest from areas you know haven't been treated with chemicals, and remember that helping control this invasive species is actually an environmental good deed!
confusionNotes: The paired flowers aging from white to yellow make this species unmistakable among honeysuckles - native honeysuckles typically have consistently colored flowers and don't show this dramatic color change on the same plant.
contextualKnowledge: Though beautiful and fragrant, Japanese honeysuckle is considered one of New England's most problematic invasive plants. It was originally brought from Asia as an ornamental vine in the 1800s but escaped cultivation and now smothers native forest understory plants across the region.
compareHints: Japanese honeysuckle is unique among New England honeysuckles for its white-to-yellow color change and semi-evergreen leaves. Native species like American fly-honeysuckle have consistently yellow flowers and fully deciduous leaves, while other non-native honeysuckles like Morrow's and Tatarian are upright shrubs rather than vines.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike the invasive Japanese, Morrow's, and Tatarian honeysuckles that dominate many New England areas, American fly-honeysuckle has distinctively paired berries and a much more restrained growth habit.
Unlike native fly honeysuckles which have flowers in clusters and blue or black berries, Morrow's honeysuckle has flowers and berries strictly in pairs with red fruit.
Unlike native American fly-honeysuckle which stays small and has paired flowers on long stalks, Amur honeysuckle grows into a large shrub with flowers sitting directly on the branches.
Among New England honeysuckles, coral honeysuckle is the only one with scentless, coral-red tubular flowers and that distinctive leaf-fusion around the stem.
Among New England's honeysuckles, glaucous honeysuckle is the only climbing species with that distinctive waxy blue-green leaf coating and cup-forming fused upper leaves.
Unlike our native fly honeysuckles which have flowers in clusters and blue or black berries, Tatarian honeysuckle always has paired flowers and red berries.
Mountain fly-honeysuckle differs from American fly honeysuckle by having much fuzzier leaves and preferring higher elevation habitats.
Among New England's honeysuckles, the dense coating of soft hairs immediately separates this species from smooth-leaved Japanese honeysuckle or the only slightly hairy American fly honeysuckle.
Fly honeysuckle stands out from other honeysuckles in New England by its paired red berries and shrubby growth habit - most others either climb like vines or have different colored berries.
Unlike the vigorous vining Japanese honeysuckle, winter honeysuckle is a well-behaved shrub that doesn't climb.
Unlike the more common American fly honeysuckle which prefers drier woods, swamp fly honeysuckle demands wet feet and boggy conditions.

Unlike the ubiquitous Japanese honeysuckle which blooms white to yellow and has simple opposite leaves, common honeysuckle has those distinctive fused upper leaves and more intensely fragrant flowers.
While New England has many honeysuckle species, perfoliate honeysuckle is the only one with fused upper leaves that the stem appears to grow through.
Unlike the invasive Asian honeysuckles that plague New England (Japanese, Morrow's, Amur), twinberry honeysuckle doesn't spread aggressively and has the unique twin-berry-in-red-bracts feature.
Unlike the aggressive Japanese honeysuckle that stays white then turns yellow, grape honeysuckle flowers age to pink.
Unlike its weedy relatives like Japanese honeysuckle (which climbs) or Morrow's honeysuckle (which has red berries), sweetberry honeysuckle stays compact and produces edible blue fruit.
